title: Please read the manuscript in /papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy. I was thinking about the asymptotics that need to be controlled in order to understand the problem better. I was wondering, could it be possible to explicitly factor H(t,z) at large time? We know that the zeros "crystallize" into a well defined pattern at large time, so for very large time I was wondering if it might be possible to write down an explicit expression. This could be useful, because when propagating the function you would have an exact expression to work with instead of error terms.

We know that the zeros "crystallize" into a well defined pattern at large time, so for very large time I was wondering if it might be possible to write down an explicit expression. This could be useful, because when propagating the function you would have an exact expression to work with instead of error terms.
I’ll read the manuscript and its large-time estimates, then check what the zero pattern determines about \(H(t,z)\) and what information is needed to propagate it exactly.
Please write any notes in the brainstorm folder

I’ll put the note in this investigation’s `brainstorm/notes/` folder. I found an earlier proof of the cosine limit for each fixed zero index, which gives a precise starting point for the factorization question.

The manuscript’s Jacobi coefficients give a finite-time test: after matching a cosine’s curvature at the origin, its fourth derivative still differs from \(H\)’s by a strictly positive amount. I also found an exact amplitude-and-phase formula that retains this information and identifies a growing interval where its phase labels the zeros.

Yes. **At large finite time, there is an exact factorization in which the zeros are equally spaced in a corrected phase.** That phase can be computed from the theta source without knowing any zero locations in advance.

For sufficiently large \(T\), the positive zeros \(x_k(T)\) give the exact global product
\[
\frac{H(T,z)}{H(T,0)}
=\prod_{k\ge1}\left(1-\frac{z^2}{x_k(T)^2}\right).
\]
Crystallization tells us that \(L_Tx_k(T)\to(k-\tfrac12)\pi\) for each fixed \(k\), with \(L_T\sim\tfrac14\log T\). Substituting those limiting positions gives \(\cos(L_Tz)\). The finite-time displacements carry information that matters under propagation. [Manuscript product argument](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy/manuscript/sections/hierarchy.tex:35) · [Fixed-index crystallization proof](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-3/13_contradiction_analysis/04_boundary_winding/threshold_routes/09_expanding_contour_later_collision/brainstorm/01_CAP_AT_INFINITY_20261020.md:258) · [Polymath’s all-real bound](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.12438v2#page=2)

To retain those displacements, let \(U\ge0\) have density \(e^{Tu^2}\Phi(u)/H(T,0)\), with mean \(a_T\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_T\). Define \(C_T(x)=\mathbb E_T e^{ix(U-a_T)}\). Then
\[
\boxed{\quad H(T,x)=H(T,0)\,|C_T(x)|\cos\Theta_T(x),\qquad
\Theta_T(x)=a_Tx+\arg C_T(x).\quad}
\]
On \(|x|\le1/\sigma_T\), the amplitude is at least \(1/2\) and the phase is strictly increasing for sufficiently large \(T\). Every positive zero in that interval therefore satisfies **exactly** \(\Theta_T(x_k)=(k-\tfrac12)\pi\). The interval grows with \(T\). The manuscript’s first two Jacobi links even give the leading displacement from its two-site cosine. Writing \(d=\beta_2(T)/\beta_1(T)\to0\), I get
\[
\sqrt{\beta_1(T)}\,x_k(T)
=(k-\tfrac12)\pi\,(1+d/8)+O_k(d^{3/2})
\]
for each fixed \(k\). [Derivation in the brainstorm note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy/brainstorm/notes/07_LARGE_TIME_FACTORIZATION_AND_BACKWARD_PROPAGATION_20261120.md:42)

**For propagation, the distinction is decisive.** Going backward by \(s\) multiplies each source frequency \(u\) by \(e^{-su^2}\). A single cosine has only one frequency, so its amplitude changes and every zero stays put. Propagating that cosine all the way to time zero would leave its first zero arbitrarily close to the origin as \(T\to\infty\), whereas \(H(0,0)>0\) gives the true field a fixed zero-free neighborhood there. [Exact Gaussian propagation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/manuscript/sections/01_source.tex:109)

The full finite-time product **can** be propagated exactly as a convergent limit of propagated polynomials. The phase formula also pinpoints the asymptotic quantity to control: a backward step of length \(s\) samples the Gaussian average of \(C_T\) at the complex displacement \(z+2isa_T\). That gives a concrete target beyond the observed real zero spacings. I saved both propagation formulas and their proofs in the [brainstorm folder](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy/brainstorm/notes/07_LARGE_TIME_FACTORIZATION_AND_BACKWARD_PROPAGATION_20261120.md:107).
Is there an explicit expression for x_k(T)?
I’ll check which formulas determine \(x_k(T)\) from the theta source alone, and how much the large-time limit tells us about their accuracy.

There are two useful formulas. One gives the zero near a specified lattice point by integrating over a circle whose center is known in advance. The other recovers any indexed zero from theta moments at a single all-real time, including indices outside the lattice approximation.

**Yes, as an exact definite integral.** For each fixed \(k\) and sufficiently large \(T\), the integral can be evaluated on a circle chosen in advance, without knowing any zero locations. I don’t know a finite closed form for the exact zero in standard functions.

Write \(q_k=(k-\tfrac12)\pi\). The leading approximation is \(x_k(T)\sim q_k/L_T\), where the saddle \(L_T\) is explicit in terms of the lower real branch of Lambert \(W\):
\[
L_T=-\frac14 W_{-1}\!\left(-\frac{8\pi}{T}e^{-18/T}\right)-\frac{9}{2T}.
\]
Since \(L_T\sim \tfrac14\log T\), the simplest version is \(x_k(T)\sim 4q_k/\log T\). [Saddle derivation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/manuscript/03_positive.tex:51) · [Lambert \(W\) branches](https://dlmf.nist.gov/4.13)

For the **exact finite-time location**, put \(f_T(w)=H(T,w/L_T)/H(T,0)\). Then
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
x_k(T)=\frac{q_k}{L_T}
-\frac{1}{2\pi iL_T}
\oint_{|w-q_k|=1/2}
\log\!\left(\frac{f_T(w)}{\cos w}\right)\,dw .}
\]
The circle is traversed counterclockwise. For sufficiently large \(T\), the ratio is close to \(1\) everywhere on the circle, so the principal logarithm applies. The argument principle makes the integral exactly the displacement from the lattice point. Expanding the logarithm gives a convergent series whose coefficients use theta integrals at the known point \(q_k\). [Derivation and truncation bound](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy/brainstorm/notes/07_LARGE_TIME_FACTORIZATION_AND_BACKWARD_PROPAGATION_20261120.md:113)

There is also a short approximation for that displacement using only \(T\) and \(k\). With \(\kappa_T=8TL_T-2T+36\), I get
\[
x_k(T)=
\frac{q_k}{\,L_T-2(\kappa_T+2T)/\kappa_T^2\,}
+O_k\!\left(\frac{1}{L_T^2\kappa_T^{3/2}}\right).
\]
In particular, each fixed-index zero lies slightly **to the right** of \(q_k/L_T\) for sufficiently large \(T\). For your proposed propagation of the *whole* product at one fixed all-real time, the note also gives an exact moment formula valid for every index at that same time. [First displacement](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy/brainstorm/notes/07_LARGE_TIME_FACTORIZATION_AND_BACKWARD_PROPAGATION_20261120.md:89) · [All-index moment formula](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy/brainstorm/notes/07_LARGE_TIME_FACTORIZATION_AND_BACKWARD_PROPAGATION_20261120.md:158)

Let's take the expression in terms of the loop integral. I'm curious if it could be possible to do the expansion of the logarithm and then try to perform the integrals analytically and resum all of the contributions. I know that may sound unreasonably ambitious, but please see how far you can get.
I’ll expand the logarithm on the known circle, evaluate the terms by residues, and see which of their sums can be written explicitly from the theta source.

I found a polynomial formula for every contour integral in the logarithm expansion. The sum also simplifies: after centering the source, all even cumulants contribute to the amplitude, while the odd cumulants determine the zero locations. I’m checking convergence and the first predicted change in the spacing.

The resummed formulas predict a small departure from equal spacing: at sufficiently large time, the second positive zero lies just inside three times the first. I checked the sign at \(T=1000\) with interval arithmetic. I’m now comparing the truncated sums against direct root brackets at that same time.

At \(T=1000\), four terms of the original logarithm put the second zero within \(3\times10^{-16}\) of its directly bracketed value. I also found a way to bound the error of the closed cubic expression for a range of indices that grows with \(T\).

Yes. **Every integral in the logarithm expansion can be evaluated analytically.** Summing them gives an exact, absolutely convergent expression for \(x_k(T)\) in terms of the theta source at time \(T\). The same coefficients serve all \(k\le C\sqrt T(\log T)^{3/2}\) once \(T\) is sufficiently large for the chosen \(C\). I saved the derivation in the [brainstorm note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy/brainstorm/notes/08_SUMMING_THE_LARGE_TIME_ZERO_LOOP_20261120.md).

Write \(q_k=(k-\tfrac12)\pi\). Shifting the loop to \(h=w-q_k\) gives a denominator \(\sin^n h\) in the \(n\)th logarithm term. For each Fourier mode, its residue is the explicit polynomial
\[
\operatorname{Res}_{h=0}\frac{e^{ivh}}{\sin^n h}
=\frac{i^{\,n-1}}{(n-1)!}\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(v+n-2j).
\]
Thus each original integral uses only derivatives of the theta transform at the **known** lattice point \(q_k\).

The simplification comes when the terms are summed. Let \(U\) have density \(e^{Tu^2}\Phi(u)/H(T,0)\) on the positive half-line, let \(a=\mathbb E_T U\), and let \(\gamma_j\) be its cumulants. The even cumulants enter a zero-free amplitude whose logarithm integrates to zero. Set
\[
c_j=\frac{(-1)^{j+1}\gamma_{2j+1}}{(2j+1)!\,a^{2j+1}}.
\]
Then \(a x_k(T)=Y(q_k)\), where the exact series begins
\[
Y(q)=q+c_1q^3+(3c_1^2+c_2)q^5
       +(12c_1^3+8c_1c_2+c_3)q^7+\cdots.
\]
**Every coefficient is explicit.** The coefficient of \(q^m\) is
\[
\frac1m[u^{m-1}]
 \left(1-\sum_{j\ge1}c_j u^{2j}\right)^{-m},
\]
where \([u^{m-1}]\) selects a single coefficient, so only finitely many cumulants enter at each order. All powers of \(c_1\) alone sum to a closed hyperbolic-sine expression. For the complete theta source, the exact answer obtained here is the convergent series. [Resummation and convergence proof](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy/brainstorm/notes/08_SUMMING_THE_LARGE_TIME_ZERO_LOOP_20261120.md:85) · [Lagrange inversion](https://dlmf.nist.gov/1.10.vii)

One consequence is that **the second zero lies slightly inside three times the first**. The negative third cumulant determines the direction, and the saddle calculation gives
\[
1-\frac{x_2(T)}{3x_1(T)}
\sim \frac{64\pi^2}{3T^2(\log T)^5}.
\]
This ratio detects a distortion that no adjustment of the common lattice spacing can absorb.

At \(T=1000\), direct interval brackets give \(1-x_2/(3x_1)=8.7369418009258\ldots\times10^{-8}\). Four terms of the original logarithm locate \(x_2\) within \(3.0\times10^{-16}\). The resummed series through \(q^7\) locates \(x_2\) within \(6.6\times10^{-24}\) and \(x_{40}\) within \(4.0\times10^{-11}\). For propagation, this supplies exact zero factors throughout the proven range. The global product also requires its normalization and the factors beyond that range. [Numerical enclosures](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy/numerics/08_LARGE_TIME_LOOP_RESUMMATION_20261120.json)

The goal is to get as far as possible with these explicit expressions, and then use the tools from 05_arithmetic_gap_continuation to propagate them backwards in order to maximally control the gap size. The first backward test gives a signed result. Starting from the first two zeros at \(T=1000\), the estimate proves that their gap widens throughout the descent to \(t=999\). A direct endpoint calculation with the same moment data is tighter at \(999\). I’ll report both and use the difference to guide the research plan.

The draft now connects the explicit zeros to all of the parent’s regular exterior moments. It also separates the change in mean spacing from the smaller change in gap shape. I’m checking the finished PDF, the source links, and the numerical replay before handing it over.

The analytical bridge is a single function shared by all the zeros. Let \(B\) be the complex half-line theta transform and \(J=\operatorname{Im}(\overline B B_x)\) its current. Where \(J>0\), the gap \(g=x_{k+1}-x_k\) satisfies
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\log g
=\frac1g\int_{x_k}^{x_{k+1}}\partial_x^2\log J(t,x)\,dx.
\]
This expresses the parent’s complete exterior interaction through the curvature of an explicit source quantity. Throughout the proven large-time window, the average curvature is \(-2/\kappa_t+O_C(\kappa_t^{-2})\), where \(\kappa_t\) is the saddle curvature. **The covered gaps therefore widen as time runs backward.**

For the first two positive zeros, the finite calculation proves widening at **every time from \(1000\) down to \(999\)**. Starting from \(g(1000)\approx2.34179360736\), it gives
\[
2.34232564<g(999)<2.34233193.
\]
A direct endpoint calculation using the same moments gives a narrower enclosure. The transport estimate additionally determines the direction of motion throughout the interval. Both numerical records replayed exactly, using the same underlying source evaluator. [Finite calculation and comparison](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/manuscript/finite.tex)

The research program next removes the exactly known change in mean spacing and bounds the remaining gap distortion through a signed fourth cumulant. The test is whether that cancellation tightens the complete gap enclosure or extends the same counted pair to an earlier time.
